item.description: Swiss pharmaceutical giant Lonza will build a new manufacturing facility in Bend, Oregon, with completion expected by 2029.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Lonza will build a new facility in Bend, Oregon - Completion of the structure is expected by 2029 - Initial creation of over 80 new jobs - Investment defined as significant by the pharmaceutical group
## Key facts - **What**: Construction of a new commercial manufacturing plant - When: Completion expected by 2029 - Where: Bend, Oregon, United States - Who: Lonza - Amount: Amount not yet specified
The Swiss pharmaceutical industry is further strengthening its presence and investments in the United States. The Lonza group has officially announced the construction of a new facility in Bend, in the state of Oregon. The facility will be dedicated to the commercial production of spray-dried active ingredient dispersions. According to what was communicated by the Swiss pharmaceutical company, the completion of the work is expected during the year 2029. The financial operation has been defined by company management as a significant investment, although the exact monetary amount was not disclosed in the official press release issued by the company.
### Pharmaceutical technology details
The industrial project focuses on advanced technology capable of significantly improving the solubility and, consequently, the bioavailability of active ingredients that are poorly soluble. From the perspective of the global pharmaceutical market, demand for these particular manufacturing processes is experiencing steady growth, driven by the increasing complexity in the development of modern medicines. The new facility in Oregon will allow Lonza to respond promptly to this growing demand, consolidating its technological positioning in the advanced pharmaceutical manufacturing sector on an international scale. ### Employment impact and supply chains
The launch of this major industrial project in the United States will initially lead to the creation of over eighty new highly skilled jobs in the Bend region. The strategic decision to expand production capacity overseas responds to precise logics of operational proximity to important customers and strengthening the resilience of regional supply chains. Bringing production closer to the main outlet markets allows the company to reduce the risks related to international logistics and optimise delivery times for the local pharmaceutical industry.
### Corporate Strategy and Leadership
Managing Director Wolfgang Wienand underlined the strategic importance of the transaction for the future of the Swiss group. The investment in the Bend headquarters reflects the firm belief that the United States will remain a leading source of pharmaceutical innovation and a key market for Lonza. This move fits perfectly into the company strategy called One Lonza, which aims to concentrate investments where it is possible to generate maximum economic value for customers and, ultimately, for patients. The German manager, fifty-four years old and with a past as a leading fencer, has been leading the Rhenish company since July 2024.
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [CHF-EUR exchange comparator](nav:exchange). ### Profile and history of the Lonza group
Founded in 1897, Lonza has a long industrial history rooted in Switzerland. The company was originally born in Gampel, in the Valais Canton, on the banks of the river Lonza, which represents a tributary of the Rhone. During the twentieth century, precisely in 1909, the headquarters were moved to Visp, also in the Valais Canton. Subsequently, in 1974, the company became part of Alusuisse's orbit, and then left it in 1999 and obtained an official listing on the stock exchange. In 2002 the group's main operational centre was moved to Basel.
### Position in the Swiss financial markets
Today Lonza is one of the most important industrial companies in the Confederation, with a global workforce of twenty thousand employees. During the 2025 financial year, the company recorded a total turnover of 6.5 billion Swiss francs. Thanks to these economic data and its solidity, the company is part of the SMI, the stock index that groups the twenty main securities of the Swiss financial market. item.description: Practical guide to the tax system of the Canton of Jura: three-level structure, municipal multipliers, allowable deductions and official portal for the declaration.
item.content:encoded:
## In breve - Il Cantone Giura applica imposte su tre livelli: federale, cantonale e comunale - Le aliquote cantonali sono progressive; i comuni applicano un moltiplicatore sull'imposta cantonale - Le deduzioni seguono principi federali con integrazioni cantonali specifiche - La dichiarazione si presenta online tramite il portale dell'amministrazione fiscale giurassiana
## Fatti chiave - **Cosa**: Imposte cantonali e comunali nel Cantone Giura - Quando: Scadenza dichiarazione ordinaria 31 marzo (proroghe possibili) - Dove: Cantone Giura, Svizzera - Chi: Amministrazione fiscale cantonale del Giura (Service des contributions) - Importo: Aliquote progressive per scaglioni di reddito e sostanza; moltiplicatori comunali variabili
Il sistema fiscale svizzero si articola su tre livelli: l'imposta federale diretta (IFD) gestita dall'AFC/ESTV, l'imposta cantonale e l'imposta comunale, entrambe di competenza delle amministrazioni cantonali. Nel Cantone Giura, come in tutti i cantoni, la legge fiscale cantonale definisce gli scaglioni di reddito e di sostanza, le aliquote base e le deduzioni ammesse. I comuni giurassiani applicano poi un moltiplicatore (coefficiente) sull'imposta cantonale netta per determinare l'imposta comunale dovuta.
### Struttura a tre livelli e competenze L'IFD è identica per tutti i contribuenti svizzeri e viene calcolata sull'imponibile federale. L'imposta cantonale del Giura segue una tariffa progressiva per scaglioni: all'aumentare del reddito imponibile (o della sostanza imponibile) si applicano aliquote marginali crescenti. L'imposta comunale non ha tariffa propria: è il risultato dell'imposta cantonale moltiplicata per il coefficiente comunale, che ogni comune fissa annualmente. Questa architettura rende il carico fiscale finale diverso da comune a comune pur restando all'interno dello stesso cantone.
La distinzione di competenze è rigida: AFC/ESTV gestisce IFD e IVA; le amministrazioni cantonali (nel Giura il Service des contributions) gestiscono imposte cantonali e comunali; UFAS/BSV si occupa di previdenza sociale (AVS/AI/LPP) e non fissa imposte; UST/BFS produce statistiche e non fissa aliquote. ### Aliquote, scaglioni e moltiplicatori comunali Le aliquote cantonali del Giura sono pubblicate ogni anno nel tariffario ufficiale e si applicano per scaglioni di reddito netto imponibile (dopo deduzioni) e di sostanza netta imponibile. Non esiste un'aliquota unica: il sistema è progressivo a scaglioni, quindi la prima tranche di reddito è tassata all'aliquota più bassa, la tranche successiva all'aliquota superiore, e così via. L'imposta cantonale lorda che ne risulta viene poi ridotta degli eventuali abbuoni o crediti d'imposta cantonali per arrivare all'imposta cantonale netta.
Su questa base netta si applica il moltiplicatore comunale. Ogni comune del Giura delibera annualmente il proprio coefficiente (es. 1,45; 1,60; 1,30 ecc.). L'imposta comunale = imposta cantonale netta × moltiplicatore comunale. La somma di imposta cantonale netta + imposta comunale costituisce l'imposta cantonale/comunale complessiva. A questa si aggiunge l'IFD per ottenere l'imposta totale dovuta.
### Deduzioni ammesse: principi federali e specificità cantonali Le deduzioni seguono in larga misura i principi del diritto federale armonizzato (LIFD), ma il Cantone Giura può prevedere deduzioni supplementari o parametri propri (es. deduzioni per figli, per spese di guadagno, per premi LAMal/KVG, per versamenti nel pilastro 3a, per interessi passivi, per spese mediche eccedenti una franchigia). L'elenco preciso e gli importi massimi deducibili per l'anno d'imposta in corso sono indicati nelle istruzioni ufficiali della dichiarazione d'imposta giurassiana e sul portale dell'amministrazione fiscale.
Un aspetto pratico rilevante: i contributi sociali trattenuti alla fonte (AVS/AI/IPG 5,3% a carico dipendente, AD/AC 1,1%, LAINF/LAA secondo settore, LPP sul salario coordinato con aliquote per fasce d'età) riducono il reddito lordo per determinare il reddito netto imponibile. I premi LAMal/KVG non sono contributi salariali né tasse, ma sono deducibili entro i limiti cantonali.
## Useful tools for your case To verify your within/over 20 km tax scenario, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [tax return guide](nav:tax-return). ### Deadlines, procedure and online portal The ordinary tax return must be submitted by 31 March of the year following the tax year (unless extensions are granted upon request to the tax administration). The Canton of Jura provides the official portal for electronic declaration (e-tax/online declaration), which guides the taxpayer step by step: import of pre-filled data (salary certificates, bank certificates, etc.), manual entry of missing items, automatic calculation of the taxable amount and estimated tax, sending digitally signed.
Those who do not receive the pre-filled declaration or prefer paper can request the forms from the tax administration. After submission, the office issues the final taxation with the taxation decision (Veranlagungsverfügung/ décision de taxation). You can lodge a complaint with the competent appeal authority within 30 days.
## # Taxpayer-friendly tools To simulate the impact of income, deductions, municipality of residence and family situation, the site's salary/tax calculator allows you to compare scenarios. Those who have to coordinate IFD, cantonal/municipal and social security (AVS/LPP/pillar 3a) find an overview in the payroll calculator. For the actual declaration, the direct link to the Jura e-tax portal is the fastest channel.

item.description: Karin Keller-Sutter appoints Stefan Leist as AFF Deputy Director from 1 October 2026. Already leading the Financial Policy Division since 1 March 2026.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Federal Councilor Karin Keller‑Sutter appoints Stefan Leist as deputy director of the Federal Finance Administration (AFF) from 1 October 2026 - The Federal Council was informed in the meeting of 9 September 2026 - Leist has been leading the Financial Policy and Equalisation division since 1 March 2026
## Key facts - **What**: Appointment as deputy director of the Federal Finance Administration - When: Takes office 1 October 2026, decision 9 September 2026 - Where: Federal Finance Administration, Bern - Who: Stefan Leist, 45, PhD in political economy - Importance: Key role for financial policy and inter‑cantonal equalisation
Federal Councilor Karin Keller‑Sutter, head of the Federal Department of Finance, appointed Stefan Leist as deputy director of the Federal Finance Administration (AFF) effective 1 October 2026. The decision was communicated to the Federal Council in the meeting of 9 September 2026.
### Professional background and skills Stefan Leist, 45, has many years of experience within the Federal Administration. Since 1 March 2026 he has already held the position of deputy director of the AFF and head of the Financial Policy, Financial Equalisation and Financial Statistics division. He earned a degree in political economy at the University of Bern and obtained his PhD in 2012, the year he joined the State Secretariat for Economic Affairs (SECO). Before moving to the AFF, he headed the Labour Market Analysis and Social Policy unit at SECO and was deputy head of the Economic Policy Directorate.
### The role of the AFF in the federal system The Federal Finance Administration is the central unit for managing the Confederation's finances. Its main tasks include preparing the federal budget, managing public debt, financial policy and financial equalisation between the Confederation and the cantons. The division led by Leist deals precisely with these strategic dossiers, including financial statistics that feed national fiscal policy decisions. ### Implications for Swiss financial policy The appointment of Leist comes at a time when federal financial policy must confront structural challenges: the brake on indebtedness, the equalisation of resources among cantons and the evolution of the federal direct tax. The Financial Policy, Financial Equalisation and Financial Statistics division that he leads is the analytical engine behind the proposals that the Federal Council submits to Parliament for the budget and the final accounts.
### Continuity and signals from within The fact that Leist was already deputy director of the AFF since 1 March 2026 signals operational continuity: the promotion to deputy director formalises a role that he has de facto exercised for six months. His career at SECO, where he acquired expertise on the labour market and economic policy, brings to the AFF a transversal vision that links federal revenues, social spending and employment dynamics. This hybrid profile is rare at the top of the financial administration and could strengthen coordination between the Federal Department of Finance and the Federal Department of Economic Affairs, Education and Research.
### Financial equalisation: the hot dossier Among the most sensitive dossiers that Leist's division handles is the financial equalisation 2028‑2035, currently in preparation. The mechanism redistributes resources between the Confederation and the cantons and between wealthy cantons and cantons with lower fiscal capacity. Any adjustment of the parameters — fiscal power, burden indices, compensation for cases of rigidity — has direct effects on cantonal budgets and, by reflection, on cantonal and municipal taxes that citizens and businesses pay. The continuity guaranteed by Leist, who knows the UST/BFS statistical models underlying the calculations, reduces the risk of technical discontinuity in the next cycle.
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [CHF-EUR exchange comparator](nav:exchange). ### What changes for those who live and work in Switzerland The appointment does not directly change rates or deadlines for taxpayers. However, stability at the top of the AFF is a necessary condition for the budget, final account and equalization processes to respect constitutional deadlines. Delays or uncertainties in these processes have an impact on cantonal estimates and, ultimately, on the taxes that residents — including border workers — pay at the cantonal and municipal levels.
### How to follow the work of the AFF Financial policy documents, equalisation reports and financial statistics are published on the AFF and UST/BFS website. item.title: F-35: Amherd Risks Liability for Extra Costs
item.description: CdG ascertains that Amherd knew of the F-35 cost risks months earlier. Three-year prescription expiring, Wyssmann asks for an interruption.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - The CdG established that Amherd was aware of the risks of extra costs on the F-35s months before informing the Federal Council. - No final price was ever set for the purchase of the 36 jets. - UDC National Councillor Wyssmann is asking to block the statute of limitations for potential liability actions. - The three-year deadline to take legal action may expire soon.
## Key facts - **What**: Investigation by the National Council's Committee of Administration regarding the purchase of the F-35s. - When: Report recently published; three-year statute of limitations is running. - Where: Bern, federal level. - Who: Former Federal Councillor Viola Amherd, CdG, National Councillor Rémy Wyssmann (UDC), Federal Council. - Amount: Potential damage not yet specified; previous Bischof case involved 112,500 francs. - Legal basis: Art. 5 para. 3 of the Ordinance on the Liability Act.
### The CdG investigation and its findings The National Council's Committee of Administration (CdG) has concluded its investigations into the methods used to purchase the 36 F-35 jets. According to the report, former Federal Councillor Viola Amherd was aware, months before informing the Federal Council, of the risk of additional costs. Furthermore, a final price for the contract was never set. Amherd, currently in Oslo for the funeral of Norwegian King Harald V, has so far chosen silence and has not responded to journalists' requests.
### The debate on legal liability In Bern, the issue of personal liability is at the center of political debate. UDC National Councillor Rémy Wyssmann had asked a year ago for the Federal Council to adopt 'all necessary measures' so that potential civil liability claims against Amherd and the officials involved would not fall under the statute of limitations. At the time, the Federal Council had recommended rejecting the request, arguing that there were 'no sufficient concrete indications either of the presence of damage, or of unlawful conduct.' However, it had assured that the competent authorities would evaluate legal actions should such indications emerge.
### Jurisdiction and precedents According to Article 5, paragraph 3, of the Ordinance on the Liability Act, jurisdiction for potential legal actions against Amherd lies with the Federal Council as a whole; for the officials involved, liability falls under the Department of Defense. A historical precedent is represented by the case of Councillor of States Pirmin Bischof (Centre), who in the 1990s was held personally responsible for the failure of the Solothurn Cantonal Bank and paid 112,500 francs. Former Socialist National Councillor Pierre-Alain Fridez considers the investigation insufficient and calls for the establishment of a parliamentary committee of inquiry, extending the in-depth analysis to the choice of the F-35 model.

item.title: Bribery money: the Swiss dilemma
item.description: Return of illicit funds: a long and complex process. Why does Switzerland not oblige banks to pay directly to the injured states?
item.content:encoded:
## In Brief - The return of money from corruption is a long and complex process - Switzerland does not obligate banks to pay directly to harmed States - It is a central issue for Swiss federal banking regulation
## Key Facts - **What**: Return of funds from corruption - When: September 2026 - Where: Switzerland, federal financial center - Who: Swiss banks and federal authorities - Problem: Complex process; lack of obligation for direct payment to States
As of September 2, 2026, the issue of returning money from corruption remains one of Switzerland's Achilles' heels. The process is known for being complex and lengthy, raising a fundamental question about Swiss banking regulation: why doesn't the State impose on banks to pay these sums directly to the States that have been harmed?
The question reveals a tension between the regulatory role of federal authorities and the operational methods of Swiss credit institutions. Banks manage significant flows of money, including those related to anti-corruption proceedings. However, the absence of an explicit obligation for direct payment to damaged countries suggests a regulatory framework still evolving, where the balance between national sovereignty and international compliance remains delicate.
### The Core Issue of Restitution
The complexity of the process is not accidental. The return of funds from corruption involves multiple administrative steps: identification of accounts, seizure, legal verification, international negotiations and finally the actual transfer. Each phase requires time and coordination among banks, Swiss authorities and foreign governments. The source of the debate lies in the fundamental question: if Switzerland intends to position itself as a reliable financial center committed to the fight against corruption, why not simplify the process by requiring banks to pay directly?
This question touches both technical and political aspects of federal regulation. The issue raised in September 2026 highlights a debate that goes beyond the simple technical question: it is a reflection on the very nature of the Swiss financial system. If banks are custodians of international capital, and Switzerland promotes itself as a center of integrity and transparency, then what logic underlies the maintenance of such an articulated and lengthy restitution system? It reflects a complex negotiation between national sovereignty, international norms and the reputation of the Swiss financial center. Explore how tax declarations and financial transparency are related to banking compliance. ### The perspective of federal regulation
The regulation of Swiss banks falls under federal control, primarily through institutions such as FINMA (Federal Financial Markets Supervision Authority) and SNB (Swiss National Bank). These authorities supervise compliance with anti-corruption and compliance regulations. However, the current regulatory framework does not provide for an explicit obligation to directly transfer funds to countries harmed by corruption offenses.
Why this gap? The reasons can be multiple: legal complexity, state sovereignty in fund management, parallel civil proceedings, or political considerations. Switzerland has a long tradition of neutrality, which also influences decisions on the management of international funds. At the same time, the Swiss financial market must maintain global credibility in a context where transparency and compliance are increasingly essential.
The issue raised in September 2026 is not new, but receives renewed attention for the central role that transparency and banking compliance play in international commercial relations. Switzerland's trading partners, particularly the European Union and the United States, exert constant pressure for stricter regulations on the return of illicit funds.
### Implications for Swiss banks and institutions
Swiss banks operate in an increasingly rigorous compliance context. Even without an explicit obligation to transfer directly, they must comply with anti-money laundering (AML), Know Your Customer (KYC) and enhanced due diligence regulations. Every transaction related to potentially illicit funds is subject to strict verification.
This situation creates a dilemma: on the one hand, banks must protect their reputation by operating with maximum transparency; on the other, the long and complex restitution process reflects a system still in the process of optimization. Consequently, transparency in banking operations not only protects Swiss institutions but also helps consolidate Switzerland's reputation as a reliable partner in the fight against global corruption. If you work in the financial sector, are an international entrepreneur, or simply want to better understand how Switzerland addresses corruption, various information paths are available. First: consult FINMA's official guidelines on the website of the Federal Financial Market Supervisory Authority. FINMA publishes circulars, standards, and recommendations on banking compliance. Second: contact your Swiss bank directly, which has dedicated teams for regulatory compliance matters.
Third: follow federal parliamentary debates. Although the repatriation issue is mainly technical, the Federal Council and Parliament periodically revisit regulations on the management of illicit funds. These discussions can lead to reforms that simplify the repatriation process. Fourth: for those operating in high-risk sectors (import/export, construction, public procurement), anti-corruption due diligence is mandatory. Documenting your suppliers, beneficial owners of contracts, and financial flows is essential.
### Concrete steps for solid compliance
If you hold an account at a Swiss bank or manage international transactions:
1. **Verify your bank**: ensure that you operate according to the highest compliance standards. [Swiss banks](nav:banks) are subject to constant FINMA supervision.
2. Documentation: keep all documentation relating to your transactions. In case of investigations into potentially illicit funds, traceability is essential.
3. Accurate declarations: complete tax declarations with maximum precision, indicating all sources of income and international assets.
4. Specialized advice: if involved in complex cross-border transactions, consult experts in banking compliance and anti-corruption regulations.
The issue of returning money from corruption remains a space where Switzerland finds itself balancing operational efficiency, national sovereignty, and global credibility. Swiss banks will continue to operate under stringent regulations, but the debate on how to simplify the repatriation process remains open. item.title: Federal Council reorganises extra-parliamentary committees
item.description: The Federal Council adopts the message on the reorganization of extra-parliamentary committees: 3 dissolved, 7 merged into 2 structures; savings ~ CHF 100,000 per year from 2028.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Federal Council adopts message on reorganization of extraparlimentary commissions on 9 September 2026 - Dissolution of 3 commissions, merger of 7 into 2 new structures; savings of approximately 100,000 CHF per year - Commissions reduced by 16% from 1 January 2028; amendment to federal law on government and administration
## Key facts - **What**: Message on reorganization of extraparlimentary commissions (review 2025) - When: Adopted 9 September 2026; entry into force 1 January 2028 - Who: Swiss Federal Council - Where: Federal Administration level - Amount: Approximately 100,000 CHF savings per year - Impact: 16% reduction in commissions from 2028
On 9 September 2026, the Federal Council adopted the message on the reorganization of extraparlimentary commissions within the framework of the 2025 review. The decision provides for the dissolution of three commissions and the merger of seven others, which will become two unified structures. The measure will generate savings of almost 100,000 francs per year starting from 1 January 2028.
### The dissolved commissions
Three extraparlimentary commissions will be dissolved: the Commission for the Dissemination of Swiss Education Abroad, the Federal Consumer Commission and the Federal Housing Commission. The Federal Council has furthermore decided to dissolve two additional commissions and to reorganize the Federal Accreditation Commission. The tasks of the dissolved commissions will be reallocated to other competent federal offices or eliminated if superseded.
### The mergers: five unified examination commissions
The five Examination Commissions in Chiropractic, Veterinary Medicine, Dentistry, Human Medicine and Pharmacy will be merged into a single structure: the Examination Commission for University Medical Professions. A rationalization that concentrates the control and certification of medical professions in a single body. At the same time, the Federal Labour Commission and the Federal Tripartite Commission for Measures Accompanying the Free Movement of Persons will become the Tripartite Labour Commission of the Confederation, creating a new structure that brings together expertise in labour policy and freedom of movement.
### Regulatory amendment and overall numbers
The Federal Council has provided for an amendment to the Federal Law on the Organization of the Government and the Administration in order to clarify the purpose of extraparlimentary commissions and regulate their communication with members and bodies of Parliament. Taking into account all the dissolutions decided and those submitted to Parliament, the total number of extraparlimentary commissions will decrease by 16 per cent from 1 January 2028. The examination of a possible reorganization of the Swiss Science Council must instead be carried out by the end of 2027. ### The four-year verification cycle of commissions
The purpose, responsibilities and composition of extra-parliamentary commissions are reviewed globally every four years, on the occasion of their complete renewal. The Federal Council has completed the consultation on the matter and has noted the results before adopting the message on reorganization. This regular cycle allows the Confederation to continuously adjust the administrative structure to current operational needs and to eliminate overlaps of competencies that have accumulated over time.
### Administrative rationalization and impact on the federal budget
Savings of approximately 100,000 francs annually reflect a logic of administrative efficiency and control of public spending. Fewer organizations mean lower management costs, meetings, secretariats and personnel. The overall reduction of 16 percent of commissions from 2028 represents a step towards broader rationalization of the federal apparatus, although the amounts involved remain limited on a national scale. The reform is part of a more general strategy to streamline federal bureaucracy.
### Consolidation of medical professions and labor policy
The two most significant mergers reflect an integrated vision of the federal government. The reunification of the five examination commissions into a single commission simplifies oversight of chiropractic, veterinary medicine, dentistry, human medicine and pharmacy, creating consistency in protocols and examination procedures. Similarly, the new tripartite Labor Commission brings together the Federal Labor Commission and the former tripartite commission on freedom of movement, creating a leaner structure to address labor issues at the federal level.
### The role of Parliament in ratifying the reform
The Federal Council's message will be submitted to deputies and senators for approval of the regulatory amendment and related measures. The two chambers will be able to examine the proposals in their specialized commissions, formulate observations and propose amendments before entering into force. Parliament has final decision-making powers over the revised federal law on the organization of Government and Administration.
## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare [CHF-EUR exchange options](nav:exchange) and [banks for cross-border workers](nav:banks). ### Legislative timeline and crucial deadlines
The message was formally adopted by the Federal Council on September 9, 2026. From this point on, the text will follow the ordinary parliamentary procedure: examination in the commissions of the National Council and the States, discussions in plenary sessions, and possible exchanges between the two chambers. Entry into force is scheduled for **January 1, 2028**, allowing sufficient time for organizational transition within the Federal Administration and enabling the involved commissions to adapt their internal structures.
### Operational impact on involved commissions
Dissolved commissions will cease their regular activities. Their tasks will be reallocated to other competent federal offices or eliminated if superseded by new administrative dynamics. Merged commissions will have to carry out a significant internal reorganization: the new Commission for the Examination of University Medical Professions will have to coordinate the examination protocols of the five medical professions, while the Tripartite Labor Commission will have to integrate the two previous bodies with common decision-making structures and processes. During the transition period until January 1, 2028, current members will remain in office according to the procedures established by the Federal Council.
### Future review of the Swiss Science Council
The Federal Council has postponed the examination of a possible reorganization of the Swiss Science Council by the end of 2027. This signals that the administrative review is not yet concluded and that other government bodies could undergo similar changes in the coming months. The review of the Swiss Science Council will follow its own timeline and will be communicated later.
### Monitoring and access to official documents
Those interested in following legislative progress can consult the Federal Administration's website (admin.ch) or Fedlex to access official documents. The federal law on reorganization and the complete message are available online in PDF format. The amendment to the federal law on the organization of the Government and the Administration will have limited impact for the average citizen, but represents an important update for those who interact with federal commissions, work in federal offices involved in the reorganization, or closely follow Swiss administrative governance dynamics.

item.title: St Gallen sick pay premiums: reduction and models
item.description: Mandatory LAMal in Switzerland: CHF 300–2500 deductibles, alternative models and cantonal procedure for the subsidy. How to request the reduction and deadlines.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - LAMal is compulsory health insurance for all residents in Switzerland - Adult deductibles: CHF 300, 500, 1000, 1500, 2000, 2500 (policyholder's choice) - Premiums vary by canton, region and chosen model (standard, HMO, high deductible) - Premium reduction: cantonal subsidy financed with local taxes, based on income/wealth
## Key facts - **What**: LAMal (compulsory health insurance, Swiss compulsory health insurance) - Who: All residents (Swiss and foreign citizens, to be taken out within 3 months of arrival) - Type: Private insurance with per-capita premiums, NOT a tax nor a payroll contribution - Deductibles: CHF 300-2500 per year for adults (fixed by federal law) - Reduction: Cantonal subsidy for low/medium-low incomes, mandatory annual request
### What is LAMal and the role of the reduction
Compulsory health insurance (LAMal in Italian, KVG in German and French) is the cornerstone of the Swiss healthcare system. All residents—Swiss and foreign citizens—are required to take out a policy with an authorised private insurer within three months of arriving in Switzerland.
Unlike in other countries, LAMal is neither a tax nor a payroll contribution, but a genuine insurance with individual premiums paid directly to the insurer each month. Premiums vary strongly according to the canton of residence, region and the chosen coverage model (standard model, HMO, high deductible).
A central aspect of LAMal is the premium reduction, also called a subsidy. It is a contribution financed by the cantonal and municipal taxes, intended for people with low or medium-low income. It is not optional: if you are entitled, you must actively apply to the municipality or the competent cantonal office.
### Deductibles: a strategic choice
Deductibles are fixed by federal law. Adults can choose between CHF 300, 500, 1000, 1500, 2000, 2500 per year. The deductible is the first amount the policyholder pays out-of-pocket in a calendar year; above that threshold, the insurer covers 90% of costs up to an annual maximum, then 100%.
The choice of deductible directly influences the monthly premium: lower deductibles (CHF 300) lead to higher monthly premiums; higher deductibles (CHF 2500) reduce the premium. The decision depends on personal health needs. Those with chronic conditions or expecting frequent care are better off choosing a low deductible; young and healthy individuals can opt for a high deductible to save on the annual premium.
### Alternative models
Besides the standard model with full access to specialists, LAMal allows enrolment in alternative models: the HMO model requires joining an HMO network and selecting a primary care physician, with access to specialists only by referral. There is also the compulsory primary-care model outside structured networks. These models generally have lower premiums than the standard model. The model choice is annual (like the deductible) and can be changed by 30 November for effect from 1 January.
### Entitlement to the cantonal reduction
Each canton administers its own reduction programme independently. There is no single federal income threshold: each canton sets its own limits based on gross income, wealth and personal situation (single, couple, dependents). In general, the reduction targets low-to-medium incomes, with coverage varying according to the canton’s generosity and the income bracket. ### When and how to apply for the reduction
The premium reduction application must be submitted each year to the municipality of residence or directly to the competent cantonal office (varies by canton). Deadlines are cantonal—generally by March, June, or November of the previous year to cover the following fiscal year—so it is essential to check the deadline with your own municipality.
To submit the application you need: - Federal tax return of the previous year - Salary certificate from the employer or self‑employment income declaration - Asset declaration (real estate, bank accounts, securities) - Cantonal application form, available at the municipality or downloadable from the official website
Many cantons provide online calculators to estimate eligibility for the reduction before filing the official application. It is advisable to use them to verify whether you qualify, so as to avoid surprises.
Once the application is submitted, the cantonal office processes it usually within 2–6 weeks. If approved, the policyholder receives a letter with the monthly subsidy amount. Usually, the subsidy is granted as a direct discount on the policy (the policyholder pays the reduced premium) or as a direct reimbursement from the canton to the policyholder.
### The subsidy is not automatic and must be renewed every year
A common mistake is to believe that the reduction, once obtained, continues automatically in subsequent years. This is not the case: the subsidy expires on 31 December each year. To keep it, you must file a new application with updated documentation (latest income, assets) following the same cantonal deadlines.
If you do not renew the application, starting 1 January of the following year you lose the reduction and must pay the full premium. Many people forget the deadline—it is wise to mark the cantonal deadline for submission in your calendar.
If your income rises and exceeds the cantonal threshold (for example, due to a promotion, marriage to a spouse with higher income, inheritance), the entitlement to the subsidy is withdrawn. In this case you do not need to submit a new application; the office will communicate the withdrawal ex officio.
### Variability between cantons and choice strategies
Although LAMal is regulated at the federal level, cantonal policies on the reduction vary greatly. Some cantons are more generous in coverage; others are more conservative. This variability reflects cantonal fiscal and social differences and the Swiss federalist principle.
Anyone moving between cantons should expect a change in average premiums and subsidy entitlement. It is reasonable to consult the information of the new canton before moving to assess the impact on LAMal. Those dissatisfied with their health insurer have the right to switch each year (by 30 November), free of charge and without penalties. This is an opportunity to seek better premiums or models better suited to one’s needs.
## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare [CHF-EUR exchange options](nav:exchange) and [banks for cross-border workers](nav:banks). ### Step-by-step procedure for requesting the reduction
**Step 1: Verify your eligibility** Access your canton's official website (tax section, social services, or health) and consult the reduction calculator if available. Enter your gross income, assets, and personal situation data for a preliminary estimate of your eligibility.
Step 2: Gather the documentation Prepare a copy of the previous year's federal tax declaration, employer salary certificate or self-employment income statement, asset documentation (bank statements, property certificates), current LAMal policy number.
Step 3: Obtain the cantonal form Download the application form from your municipality or canton website, or pick it up at the municipal office. Forms vary slightly by canton.
Step 4: Complete and submit Complete the form with the required information. Attach all original documentation or certified copies. Submit to the municipal office or send by registered mail before the cantonal deadline.
Step 5: Application processing The cantonal office processes the application, typically within 2–6 weeks. If approved, you receive a letter with the monthly subsidy amount and payment details.
Step 6: Annual renewal Don't forget: repeat the process every year before the cantonal deadline. Keep receipts of submission and approval letters.
### What to do if the amount is less than expected
If you believe the subsidy calculation is incorrect or insufficient, you have the right to contest the decision. Contact the cantonal office for clarification, providing your current data (income changes, assets, personal situation). Some cantons also provide an administrative appeal procedure if you disagree with the decision.
### Critical deadlines to mark
Each year the LAMal calendar sets fixed deadlines: November 30 is the deadline for changing health insurance providers (effective January 1); the cantonal deadline for reduction applications varies by canton (November, December, January, March, June—check yours). Don't wait until the last minute: administrative deadlines are strict, and delays result in loss of eligibility for that year.
### Useful tools for comparing and deciding
Consult the following resources for canton-specific information: official municipal website (Tax or Social Services section), cantonal office responsible for premium reductions, [LAMal calculator and insurance provider comparison tool](nav:health) to check premiums and alternative plans, cantonal toll-free number or contact email for administrative questions.
Remember: the reduction is not automatic. Those eligible must actively request it every year before the deadline set by their canton. Don't wait: the subsidy typically takes effect the month following approval of your application, not retroactively.

item.description: Registration in the trade register, legal forms, minimum capital and insurance obligations: everything you need to start a business in the canton of Schwyz.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Opening a business in Schwyz requires registration with the cantonal business register - Legal forms: sole proprietorship, general partnership, joint-stock company (AG), limited liability company (GmbH) - Insurance obligations and taxes vary based on the chosen form
## Key facts - **What**: registration with the Schwyz Cantonal business register - Where: Schwyz Canton (central Switzerland) - Who: prospective entrepreneurs, both residents and non-residents - When: before starting the business - Legal forms: sole proprietorships, general partnerships, joint-stock companies (AG), limited liability companies (GmbH) - Obligations: professional liability insurance, VAT registration if turnover exceeds the federal threshold
Starting a business in the Canton of Schwyz involves a series of well-defined administrative and financial steps. The choice of legal form — sole proprietorship, general partnership, joint-stock company (AG) or limited liability company (GmbH) — represents the first crucial step, as it determines both the entrepreneur's civil liability and tax and pension obligations. Registration with the cantonal business register is mandatory before starting the business and constitutes the legal foundation of the enterprise.
### Legal forms and liability
The choice of legal form is not merely bureaucratic: it directly impacts the entrepreneur's asset protection and management costs. A sole proprietorship, the simplest and most common form, makes the owner personally and unlimitedly liable for business debts. By contrast, a GmbH or AG separate personal assets from business assets, limiting liability to the capital contributed. This distinction is essential for assessing the enterprise's risk profile during the planning phase.
### Tax and pension implications
Cantonal taxes vary significantly among Swiss cantons. Schwyz, like every canton, applies its own income and capital tax rate. Those starting a business must pay contributions for social insurance (old-age, disability, and unemployment insurance) on a minimum basis, even if they have no employees. For a sole proprietor, the total contribution rate is approximately 10.6% of net income (5.3% employee + 5.3% employer). If you have employees, contributions increase further with accident insurance and occupational pension insurance. Occupational pension insurance is mandatory if the coordinated salary exceeds CHF 21,330 annually; the contribution rate ranges from 7% to 18% depending on age. For more details on your pension situation, consult the [pension guide](nav:pension). ### Registration in the commercial register: procedure and documents
Registration in the commercial register of Canton Schwyz is the fundamental administrative act. Depending on the legal form chosen, the canton requires specific documentation: articles of association for companies, declaration of business for sole proprietorships, and identification of the entrepreneur. Registration costs and processing times vary based on the complexity of the structure; it is advisable to consult the competent cantonal office for updated details on forms, fees and specific timeframes.
### Minimum capital and initial deposits
Minimum capital is not standardized at the national level for all legal forms. A sole proprietorship does not require formal minimum capital, offering maximum flexibility for small entrepreneurs. A joint-stock company (SA) generally requires at least CHF 100,000 (half of which must be paid at the time of incorporation), while a limited liability company (SAGL) requires at least CHF 20,000. However, cantonal rules may vary; Schwyz may have specific provisions that must be verified with the competent cantonal authority before proceeding with incorporation.
### Insurance and tax obligations after registration
Every entrepreneur is required to obtain professional liability insurance, the cost of which depends on the sector of activity and risk profile. Furthermore, if turnover exceeds the VAT threshold (CHF 100,000 annually), registration in the federal VAT register is mandatory. Anyone employing employees must register with SUVA (Swiss National Accident Insurance Institution) for accident insurance (LAA/LAINF). Contributions for social security (AVS/AI/IPG) and accident insurance depend on the contractual situation and must be paid regularly. Cantonal income and capital taxes vary by canton; Schwyz has its own rates and systems. Finally, if you employ employees resident in Switzerland, they must be registered with private health insurance (LAMal) within three months of arrival in Switzerland (if foreign nationals) or at the time of employment (if residents). To understand how Swiss payslip management affects accounting, consult our [payslip guide](nav:payslip).
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### Practical Procedure: From Idea to Registration
1. **Define the legal form** based on the risk profile, complexity, and business growth plans. 2. Gather the documents required by the canton: articles of incorporation (for companies), personal identification, property documents or premises, and any sector-specific authorizations. 3. Contact the Schwyz canton's commercial register office to verify canton-specific requirements, updated forms, and registration fees. 4. Submit a complete registration application with documentation and pay the required registration fees. 5. Wait for registration confirmation (timelines vary; typically from a few days to several weeks). 6. Register with the Federal VAT Register at the Federal Customs Administration (if your turnover requires it). 7. Register with the cantonal tax office and communicate your business start date for income tax purposes.
### Ongoing Obligations and Compliance
After registration, the entrepreneur must comply with a series of obligations: maintain records and accounting (in accordance with the Swiss Code of Obligations), annual cantonal tax returns, regular payment of AVS/AI/IPG and LPP contributions (for yourself or employees, depending on the structure), maintenance of professional insurance, and, if employing staff, registration with SUVA and compliance with federal labor regulations (maximum working hours of 45 or 50 hours per week depending on the sector, minimum vacation of 4 weeks, probationary period and termination with notice periods of 1-3 months according to seniority).
### Where to Get Information and Useful Resources
The Schwyz canton publishes registration guidance through its commercial register office. At the federal level, the Federal Customs Administration manages the VAT Register, while the cantonal AVS/AI fund provides information on social security and contributions. For questions about social security and salary contributions, you can consult the [salary calculator](nav:calculator) to estimate the impact of AVS/AI/IPG and LPP contributions on your net earnings. For complex accounting, cantonal tax, and legal structure matters, consult a local tax or business advisor specialized in Schwyz.

item.title: Working at SECO: apprenticeship and internship opportunities
item.description: SECO, a federal agency with over 900 employees, offers AFC apprenticeships, SMC internships and university internships. Discover the profiles you are looking for and how to apply.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - SECO counts over 900 employees distributed across three Swiss offices plus ~30 detached abroad - Offers AFC apprenticeships, SMC internships and university stages in stimulating environments - Sought profiles: commercial employees, digital business developers, IT specialists
## Key facts - **Who**: SECO (State Secretariat for the Economy), Swiss federal agency - What: AFC apprenticeship, SMC internship, university stage - Where: Three offices in Switzerland + approximately 30 employees detached abroad - Workforce: Over 900 employees and managers - Sought profiles: Commercial employees, digital business developers, IT specialists - Mandate: Economic policy, international trade, national labor market
---
SECO, the State Secretariat for the Economy of the Federal Department of the Economy, is among the principal employers in the Swiss federal public sector. With over 900 employees and managers distributed across three offices on the national territory and approximately 30 professionals detached to Swiss representations abroad, the agency represents a significant employment hub for those intending to begin or develop a career in the federal economic and administrative sector.
### What opportunities does SECO offer
SECO has structured a multi-faceted recruitment path that includes three main channels of access. AFC apprenticeships are divided into three specializations: commercial employees, digital business developers and IT sector specialists. The agency also welcomes trainees from commercial schools (SMC programs — company internships). Candidates with university education (students or recent graduates) can apply for stages of varying duration. According to SECO, interns 'put their knowledge into practice, assume various responsibilities and work on a series of concrete projects' within the agency.
### The work environment at SECO
The institution emphasizes that the value of the application is not limited to compensation, but to the work environment and the significance of the role. SECO offers 'a stimulating work environment, where responsibility, open-mindedness and personal initiative are valued'. Those who join SECO have the concrete opportunity to contribute to shaping Swiss economic policy. This is not merely marketing, but reflects the agency's actual mandate: managing commercial policy, the national labor market, Swiss competitiveness, international economic relations. SECO's organizational structure, with three dislocated offices and an international network, allows employees to operate in diverse professional environments, acquiring experience both at the federal administrative level and in strategically-focused national contexts. ## SECO in the Swiss Federal Labor Landscape
SECO is not an isolated employer. It is part of the Swiss federal apparatus which, together with dozens of other offices and agencies, manages economic, commercial, labor, tax, and social security policy. Work at SECO has a peculiarity: it is not operational in the traditional sense (e.g., management of public services directly serving citizens), but rather **strategic and decision-making**. Those working at SECO contribute to the definition of policies that impact Swiss competitiveness in international markets, the national labor market (unemployment, job protection, collective agreements), bilateral and multilateral trade agreements, and economic regulation at the federal level. This distinguishes SECO from many other employers: it does not perform ordinary administrative functions, but actively contributes to 'shaping economic policy', as the institution itself declares.
### Geographic Network and International Opportunities
SECO has three offices in Switzerland and a network of approximately 30 people deployed in various countries. This means that a SECO employee has concrete opportunities to develop international experience by working at Swiss trade missions, diplomatic representations, or multilateral agencies. For an apprentice or intern, this represents a differential compared to many other training paths: experience is not limited to a single office, but can expand to the international level, acquiring global business skills.
Working as a federal employee in Switzerland also means access to competitive working conditions, guaranteed social security (AVS/LPP), and the possibility to live in any Swiss canton or city where SECO has offices. To compare cost of living and wages among major Swiss cities, consult our [cost of living calculator](nav:cost-of-living).
### Required Profiles and Skill Gaps
SECO specifically seeks digital business developers and IT specialists. This reflects a reality of the Swiss federal public sector: even traditional government agencies are investing in digital transformation. The absence of prior experience requirements (being apprenticeships and internships) suggests that SECO is interested in attitude and potential rather than consolidated expertise. The environment values 'responsibility, open-mindedness, and personal initiative' — transversal skills that signal a culture of learning and self-management.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ## How to Apply to SECO
The application procedure for positions at Swiss federal agencies follows precise steps. The first step is to consult the official SECO website (www.seco.admin.ch) where open positions, selection criteria, and application forms are published. Once you have identified the opportunity of interest, it is necessary to verify the specific requirements: each AFP apprenticeship profile has its own prerequisites (e.g., for digital developers: problem-solving skills; for IT: basic programming or IT competencies). Subsequently, prepare the required documentation — typically CV, cover letter, school certificates (for apprentices) or university diploma (for interns). Finally, submit your application following the procedures outlined in the published call for applications.
### Freelance Translators and Complementary Opportunities
SECO also has a network of freelance translators working in Swiss official languages (Italian, French, German) and other languages. The agency's language services provide various specialized services and maintain constant contact with translation and interpreting professionals. If you are specialized in translation and wish to collaborate with a federal agency, this channel represents an opportunity for external collaboration. Details about this network are available from SECO's language services.
### Next Steps
If you are interested in a career in the Swiss federal economic sector, do not wait: the public labor market is competitive, but SECO represents a concrete opportunity for placement in a strategic context. Consult our [salary calculator](nav:calculator) to estimate remuneration in the Swiss federal public sector, and discover other positions on the [job opportunities](nav:jobs) portal to compare with offers in the private and cantonal sectors.

item.title: YUMO, UBS platform for financial education
item.description: UBS launches YUMO, a free platform to teach young people how to manage money, savings and investments. Available in 4 languages in Switzerland.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - UBS launches YUMO, a free platform for financial education - Available in German, French, Italian and English - Aimed at young Swiss people, with content for every age
## Key facts - **What**: YUMO (Your Money), a digital platform for financial and economic education - When: Announcement today via UBS press release - Where: Switzerland (free and multilingual) - Who: UBS, a leading universal bank in Switzerland - Languages: 4 languages (German, French, Italian, English) - Content: Personal budget, savings, investments, everyday economics
Switzerland has a new digital platform to teach young people the basics of finance and economics. UBS launches YUMO today, whose name derives from 'Your Money', a free tool designed especially for teenagers who want to learn how to manage money, create a personal budget and understand how savings and investments work.
'The fundamental objective is to teach how to put money at the service of one's personal projects', UBS states in a press release today. The platform is not confined to young people alone: the institution emphasizes that YUMO offers 'valuable financial and economic education content for every age, which helps better understand current events and promotes dialogue between generations'.
### How YUMO works
YUMO is based on concrete examples and interactive activities to explain the main topics of economics. The platform uses short chapters, interactive quizzes and videos to teach how to make smart financial decisions and avoid common mistakes in money management. The proposed activities allow you to better understand your relationship with money and offer practical advice for managing it in your everyday life.
Free and available in German, French, Italian and English, YUMO represents a modern evolution of a well-established tradition in Switzerland. Sergio Ermotti, CEO of UBS, emphasizes: 'As a leading universal bank in Switzerland, we are proud to carry forward a tradition that promotes financial education. It enables young people to make smart choices, strengthening their financial independence and contributing to creating a stronger and more resilient civil society'. This education is particularly important for those approaching the [Swiss job market](nav:jobs), where managing your salary and personal finances becomes a concrete priority. ### A Legacy of Financial Education in Switzerland
YUMO fits into a long tradition of financial and economic outreach to a wide Swiss audience. Back in the seventies, the Swiss Popular Bank distributed on a large scale the printed guide 'Geld und Wirtschaft' (money and economics), a document designed to bring the broad Swiss public closer to financial and economic topics using simple and accessible language. This legacy of educational commitment continues today through digital means.
The Swiss Popular Bank, which had started this project in the '70s, was acquired by Credit Suisse in 1993. Credit Suisse was subsequently absorbed by UBS starting from 2023. With YUMO, UBS resumes this historical commitment and brings it into the contemporary digital world, adapting the message to the means and needs of today's youth.
### Why Financial Education is Crucial
In Switzerland, financial literacy is an essential component of each person's ability to manage their own economic independence. Young people entering the labor market face important decisions: opening a bank account, planning savings, understanding the role of investments in building a solid financial future. The absence of accessible educational tools can lead to suboptimal financial choices and reduced capacity for personal economic planning.
The YUMO platform responds to this need by providing a knowledge base on how [the economy in everyday life](nav:cost-of-living) works in Switzerland. Understanding how savings, investments, and money management work is essential not only for the individual, but also for the overall economic well-being of society. The ability to make informed financial choices strengthens economic independence among young people and helps reduce financial disparities due to lack of knowledge.
### Intergenerational Dialogue
Although YUMO is primarily aimed at young people, UBS emphasizes that the content is valuable for all ages. This multilevel approach allows for intergenerational dialogue on finance: parents and grandparents can use the same platform to explore economic topics, facilitating family conversations on budgeting, savings, and financial planning. In a Switzerland where economics and finance are central to quality of life, these family dialogues represent added value to the overall well-being of society.
## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare [CHF-EUR exchange options](nav:exchange) and [banks for cross-border workers](nav:banks). ### How to Access YUMO
YUMO is completely free and accessible to anyone who wants to deepen their understanding of finance and economics. To access the platform, you do not need to have a UBS account: the service is public and open to all Swiss residents. The platform is available in four languages — German, French, Italian, and English — covering the main linguistic communities of the country.
To start using YUMO, simply visit UBS's digital platform and navigate to the section dedicated to financial education. No preliminary registration is required: the platform is immediately accessible. Young people can choose their own path through short chapters, interactive quizzes, and videos according to their interests and current level of knowledge.
### The Benefits for Your Financial Journey
Using YUMO offers several concrete benefits. First, it allows young people to understand how to create a solid personal budget, a fundamental step in managing money consciously. Second, the platform explains how savings and investments work, topics often neglected in traditional school education. Third, interactive activities help identify common mistakes in money management and avoid them before they become concrete problems.
The platform is particularly useful for those about to enter the Swiss labor market and will need to manage their salary, open bank accounts, and plan their personal finances. Those who understand in advance how money works are more likely to make wise financial decisions throughout their career.
### Deepen Your Financial Literacy
If you wish to complete your financial education beyond YUMO, Switzerland offers numerous resources. You can learn more about how to calculate and manage your salary using [calculators specific to your income](nav:calculator) that simulate how your earnings change based on different scenarios. Many Swiss banks, not only UBS, offer educational programs and webinars on the basics of personal finance. Furthermore, federal and cantonal bodies regularly promote financial literacy initiatives for young people and adults.
Start today with YUMO and discover how to put money at the service of your personal projects — whether it's saving for a house, planning a career, or simply understanding how to manage your money day after day.

item.title: Canton Svitto family allowances: how they work and how to claim them
item.description: In the canton of Swift, every parent with children is entitled to monthly family allowances. Here are application procedures, administrative skills, and where to check for updated amounts.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - The Canton of Swift manages its own system of family allowances with specific amounts per child - The application must be forwarded to the competent compensation fund based on the sector of work - Cheques generally start from the month of the application or from the birth of the child
## Key facts - **What**: Family allowances (children) and training allowances - Where: Canton of Svitto, Switzerland - Who: Dependent, self-employed and unemployed parents with children - Procedure: Application to cantonal clearing house - Amounts: Vary by canton and number of children (check with administration)
In Switzerland, family allowances are a fundamental social benefit guaranteed by federal legislation, but managed by each canton independently. In the canton of Svitto, as in the other cantons, the right to the allowance depends on the fulfilment of specific conditions provided for by the cantonal law: professional status of the parent, number and age of children, amount of income.
The Swiss system of family allowances provides for two main types: child allowances (paid up to a certain age of the child) and training allowances (for young people who follow vocational training or recognized school paths). In the canton of Svitto, as in any other canton, the monthly amounts, income thresholds and operating procedures are set by current cantonal legislation.
### The administrative competence and the role of the cashier ### Monthly amounts: how they vary in Switzerland
The amounts of family allowances differ significantly between Swiss cantons. Each canton independently sets the amounts per child, often with variations depending on the number of children (progressive scales) and the age of the minor. Some cantons also provide differentiated amounts for training allowances, which are usually higher than allowances for children of school age or preschool age.
Since Canton Schwyz has its own table of amounts updated annually, and such amounts are not provided by this editorial source, it is essential to consult directly the competent compensation fund or the cantonal administration website to find out the exact amounts in force in 2026. The amounts are subject to annual review and may undergo minor variations based on economic factors and cantonal policy decisions.
### Terms and deadlines for submission
At the national level, there is no fixed annual deadline for submitting a family allowance application: the request can be submitted at any time. However, the allowance generally becomes effective from the month in which the application is submitted to the competent fund. In some cantons, if the application is submitted within 6-12 months from the birth of the child, the right can be recognized retroactively from the month of birth.
In Canton Schwyz, there may be specific local regulations that establish deadlines for submission or conditions for retroactivity of the benefit. It is strongly recommended to inquire with the competent fund as soon as a child is born or your family situation changes, to avoid delays in payments and loss of arrears.
### Changes and notification of modifications
If your family or professional situation changes (increase in children, change in income, change of canton of residence, end of the young person's schooling), you must notify the compensation fund promptly, usually within 30 days. Failure to notify may result in unjustified payment of allowances, which the parent will be required to repay in full. The fund provides specific forms to communicate changes and guides the applicant on notification methods (mail, online forms, counter service).
### Frontier workers: family allowances for those working abroad
Frontier workers who work in a state of the European Union or the European Free Trade Association (EFTA, which includes Norway, Iceland, Liechtenstein) and reside in Switzerland are entitled to family allowances in their canton of residence. This is a crucial aspect for those who work in Italy and reside in Ticino: the right is protected by international agreements and Swiss federal legislation.
For frontier workers, territorial jurisdiction falls on the canton of residence (in the case of Ticino). The application procedures are identical to those for Swiss residents; however, additional documentation may be required (employment certificate from the foreign employer, proof of income in foreign currency converted to CHF). It is advisable to contact the cantonal compensation fund in advance to clarify the specific documentation required for the frontier worker status.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### Step-by-Step Procedure for Requesting the Family Allowance
1. Identify the Competent Compensation Fund The first step is to understand which fund manages family allowances for your case. This depends on two factors: the professional sector of the company where you work (industry, commerce, crafts, agriculture, public sector) and your canton of residence (Schwyz). Information can be found on the official website of the Schwyz canton administration, in the section dedicated to social rights or social security. Alternatively, you can directly contact the cantonal administrative office or ask your employer which fund is competent.
**2. Gather the Required Documentation** The fund usually requires the following documents: - Copy of parent's identity card or passport - Child's birth certificate (or extract from the birth record) or registration sheet - Documentation of professional status: payslip for employees, registration certificate with the self-employed fund for self-employed workers, unemployment insurance certificate (AI) if unemployed - For training allowances: certificate from the educational institution or apprenticeship company attesting enrollment and course duration - Any documentation of foreign income (for cross-border workers)
3. Complete the Application Form The fund provides a standard form (downloadable from the website or available at the counter). The form should include: parent's personal details, social security number (AVS number), complete details of each child (name, date of birth, AVS number), professional status and contact details. Some cantons now offer online completion via a dedicated portal.
4. Submit the Application Depending on the fund, you can send the application by ordinary mail, submit it in person at the counter, or (increasingly) complete and submit it via an online portal of the cantonal administration. Always keep a copy of the application and, if sent by mail, request a receipt of receipt.
5. Wait for the Decision The fund examines the application to verify that it is complete and that the applicant meets all requirements. If everything is in order, it approves the right to the allowance and notifies the decision to the parent. Payments usually begin the month following approval, or according to the specific timelines established by cantonal regulations.
6. Communicate Changes in Circumstances If relevant circumstances change (new child, job change, change in income, transfer to another canton, end of training for the young person), immediately inform the fund of the change. Delays in communicating can result in improper payments that you will have to repay.
### Documents and Official Contacts
For Schwyz Canton, the main references are: - Official administration website: www.sz.ch (Society / Social Security / Social Rights section) - Municipal counters: they often have information and can direct you to the competent fund - Compensation fund for your sector: available through the cantonal website or by contacting the administrative office
For cross-border workers: the social rights section of the cantonal administration can provide specific guidance on the required documentation (certificates of income in foreign currency, employment attestations from Italian employers, etc.).
### Calculation Tools and Further Information
To assess the impact of family allowances on your overall financial situation: - Use the salary and contribution calculator to see how the allowances integrate into your monthly budget - Consult the guide on [pensions and benefits (AVS/LPP)](nav:pension) to understand family allowances in the broader context of Swiss social security - Check the [cost of living in Switzerland](nav:cost-of-living) to assess how family allowances support the family budget
### Summary and Next Steps
Requesting family allowance in Schwyz Canton is not complicated, but it requires attention to procedural details and timely submission of documentation. The main recommendation is to contact the competent compensation fund as soon as a child is born or when a change in family circumstances occurs. Cantonal administrative offices are generally available to provide clarification and guide you in completing the application.
The amounts, deadlines, and specific requirements of Schwyz Canton must be verified directly with the cantonal administration, as they are subject to annual variations and regulatory updates.
